title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 89–90
description: Language contact and loanwords, false friends, easily confused meanings, and verb–noun contrasts with prefixes and particles.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied Advanced third edition. Lexical targets and senses are based on its teaching and practice material, with independently written examples, explanations and Portuguese translations; original exercises, tables and extended passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 89 sections A–C and exercises 89.1–89.6; Unit 90 sections A–C, Language help and exercises 90.1–90.3; corresponding answer-key entries and illustrated exercise targets. Selected exercise-only false friends and a noun sense are marked as such.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA only for short vocabulary targets where reasonably confident; blank IPA indicates no confidently verified transcription. Longer phrases do not imply a connected-speech transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing text and metadata are in English, apart from Brazilian Portuguese meanings in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the teaching text, tables, illustrated exercise, practice tasks and relevant answer-key entries with the uploaded source. Curated core targets and meaning contrasts, wrote independent examples and notes, and reviewed Portuguese translations and register. Checked the saved JSON against canonical keys and types, item IDs and static Word/Sentence audio rules.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 recordings. Import into VocabLab, browser-based speech synthesis and pronunciation recognition were not tested. Some loanword etymologies reflect the supplied textbook descriptions; cross-language meanings and usage may vary by region and over time.

units.title: Unit 89 — English: a global language
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 184–185 (PDF pages 186–187).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Varieties of English · word origins, borrowing and false friends
learningObjectives: Explain the Anglo-Saxon, Norse, Norman and classical influences on English vocabulary using accurate linguistic terms.
Recognise useful loanwords and match them to their meanings and typical contexts.
Identify false friends and avoid misleading cross-language similarities in meaning.
Discuss linguistic borrowing and distinguish word origins from modern patterns of use.

sectionsChecked: A · The origins of English vocabulary
B · English words from other languages
Exercises 89.1–89.6 and answer-key material, including illustrated nouns

items.pt: léxico; conjunto de palavras de uma língua
items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: The researchers compared the lexicon used in two regional varieties of English.
items.note: A specialist term for the words belonging to a language or a particular domain.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: The team traced the source of several words now used in everyday English.
items.note: Here source refers to where a word or influence originates, rather than a news source.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: Several basic English words have Anglo-Saxon roots.
items.note: The unit uses Anglo-Saxon to refer to the Old English linguistic foundation.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: The local dialect retains a word stock that differs from standard English.
items.note: A language’s collection or inventory of words; stock does not mean goods in a shop here.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: Viking settlement left traces in the names of towns and villages.
items.note: Refers to people from northern Europe whose languages contributed words to English.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: Norman influence can still be seen in English legal vocabulary.
items.note: Refers to people from Normandy who spoke a variety of French.

items.pt: enriquecer; tornar mais rico ou variado
items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: Contact with other cultures can enrich a language over time.
items.note: Often used figuratively of adding value, variety or depth to something.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: New media have had a significant impact on the way people learn languages.
items.note: An impact on something is a noticeable effect; do not replace on with in.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: The new term captures a concept that previously needed a long explanation.
items.note: An abstract idea rather than necessarily a physical object.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: The medical term has a classical origin and is related to Latin.
items.note: In this language-history context, classical refers to Latin and Ancient Greek.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: International trade can have lasting linguistic consequences.
items.note: Refers to effects on language, not to legal or economic consequences.

items.pt: empréstimo linguístico; palavra tomada de outra língua
items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: The dictionary marks the new loanword as originally Japanese.
items.note: A word adopted from another language; it need not be translated literally.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: Borrowing has helped English acquire vocabulary from many different languages.
items.note: In linguistics, a borrowing is a loanword or the process of adopting one.

items.section: A · Origins of English vocabulary
items.example: Some common English verbs are of Germanic origin.
items.note: Describes an etymological source, not necessarily a word borrowed from modern German.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: The artisan made a pendant from a polished piece of amber.
items.note: A yellow-orange fossil resin used in jewellery; the unit identifies its Arabic connection.

items.pt: escala; lista de turnos ou responsáveis
items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: Please check the duty roster before arranging your shifts.
items.note: A list showing who is assigned to tasks and when; the unit identifies a Dutch origin.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: A friendly tabby sleeps outside the library every afternoon.
items.note: A cat with a striped or mottled coat; presented as a word with a Farsi origin.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: The colourful packaging was a gimmick rather than a genuine product improvement.
items.note: A device or trick intended to attract attention, sometimes seen as superficial.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: A relaxing weekend was just the tonic she needed after the conference.
items.note: A medicine or something that restores energy or spirits; the unit gives a Greek origin.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: The baby was asleep in a wooden cot beside the bed.
items.note: British English for a small child’s bed with high sides; a word the unit traces to Hindi.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: The school informed parents about a confirmed case of mumps.
items.note: An infectious disease; typically used as a singular disease name despite its final -s.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: The restaurant hosts a karaoke night every Thursday.
items.note: A form of entertainment involving singing to recorded backing music; borrowed from Japanese.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: Booking the tickets became a real palaver because the website kept crashing.
items.note: Informal British English for excessive fuss or unnecessary trouble; the unit links it to Portuguese.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: The proposal attracted criticism from sections of the intelligentsia.
items.note: A social group of educated intellectuals; presented as a borrowing from Russian.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: We hung a hammock between two trees in the garden.
items.note: A suspended bed or seat made of fabric or netting; a word traced here to Spanish.

items.section: B · Loanwords from other languages
items.example: He wore a blue turban during the ceremony.
items.note: A head covering made from a long length of cloth; the unit identifies a Turkish source.

items.pt: falso cognato; palavra parecida com outra língua, mas de sentido diferente
items.section: C · False friends and cross-language meaning
items.example: The translator checked whether the familiar-looking term was a false friend.
items.note: A deceptive resemblance between words across languages; similar spelling does not guarantee similar meaning.

items.pt: compreensivo; solidário ao sofrimento de alguém
items.section: C · False friends and cross-language meaning
items.example: My supervisor was sympathetic when I explained the family emergency.
items.note: Means showing understanding or compassion, not simply being pleasant or likeable.

items.pt: tez; aspecto ou cor da pele do rosto
items.section: C · False friends and cross-language meaning
items.example: After a week in the sun, his complexion looked noticeably darker.
items.note: The book uses this as a Spanish–English false-friend example; it refers to facial skin.

items.pt: sem recursos; na miséria; desprovido de meios de subsistência
items.section: C · False friends and cross-language meaning
items.example: The charity offers temporary shelter to people who are destitute.
items.note: Means lacking basic necessities, not being dismissed from a job; an exercise false-friend example.

units.title: Unit 90 — Easily confused words
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 186–187 (PDF pages 188–189).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Lexical precision · similar words and verb–noun contrasts
learningObjectives: Distinguish near-synonyms and misleading word pairs by meaning, grammatical context and connotation.
Choose the correct word for frequency, continuity, light, moisture, themes, safety and security.
Contrast phrasal verbs with their noun forms, including breakout/outbreak and lookout/outlook.
Recognise how the position of up and out changes verb meanings and usage.

sectionsChecked: A · Words similar in form and close in meaning
B · Words of different form but from the same area of meaning
C · Phrasal combinations, prefix/particle pairs and Language help

items.pt: intervir; agir para resolver uma situação
items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The mediator intervened to prevent the discussion from becoming hostile.
items.note: Often neutral: step in to help, stop or change a situation. Compare interfere.

items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: I asked my colleague not to interfere in decisions outside his role.
items.note: Often disapproving: involve yourself where your involvement is unwelcome. Common patterns: interfere in something; interfere with something.

items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The monitoring system continually sent alerts throughout the afternoon.
items.note: Means repeatedly or very frequently, possibly with short breaks; often expresses annoyance.

items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The sensor recorded data continuously for twenty-four hours.
items.note: Emphasises uninterrupted activity; not interchangeable with continually when pauses matter.

items.pt: série; conjunto relacionado de programas ou eventos
items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The broadcaster commissioned a six-part series about ocean research.
items.note: A sequence of related programmes; individual episodes need not continue the same storyline.

items.pt: seriado de história contínua; narrativa em episódios
items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The detective serial ended each episode with an unresolved mystery.
items.note: A continuing storyline presented in instalments; contrasts with a thematic series.

items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: We moved our chairs into the shade to escape the midday heat.
items.note: An area sheltered from direct sunlight, often with a pleasant association.

items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The streetlights cast long shadows across the empty square.
items.note: A dark shape or area formed when an object blocks light; not simply shelter from the sun.

items.pt: à sombra de; sob a influência ou pressão de
items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The community lived in the shadow of a heavily polluting industrial complex.
items.note: Figurative: dominated, threatened or overshadowed by something; generally negative.

items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The reviewer complimented the team on the clarity of its presentation.
items.note: To express praise or admiration. Pattern: compliment someone on something; distinct from complement.

items.pt: complementar; combinar de modo a melhorar
items.section: A · Similar form, different meaning or connotation
items.example: The new course complements her existing programming skills.
items.note: To make something more complete or effective alongside something else, not praise it.

items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: Keep the compost moist while the seeds begin to grow.
items.note: Slightly wet; often desirable for food or soil, unlike unpleasant damp conditions.

items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: The basement felt damp after several days of heavy rain.
items.note: Slightly wet, often unpleasant or undesirable in rooms, clothing or weather.

items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: The central theme of the exhibition is migration and identity.
items.note: The underlying or organising idea of a work, event or discussion.

items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: The next topic on the agenda concerns the project budget.
items.note: A particular subject being talked or written about, not necessarily an overarching theme.

items.pt: segurança patrimonial; proteção contra ameaças e acesso indevido
items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: The museum improved security after several valuable objects went missing.
items.note: Protection against theft, attack or unauthorised access; contrasted with accident prevention.

items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: The laboratory introduced new safety rules for handling hot equipment.
items.note: Protection from harm, injury and accidents; often used in safety procedures.

items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: We left early to avoid heavy traffic near the stadium.
items.note: Prevent contact with an unwanted person, situation or outcome; less formal than evade in many contexts.

items.pt: escapar de; esquivar-se de; evitar com habilidade
items.section: B · Related meanings with different word forms
items.example: The suspect evaded arrest by changing vehicles several times.
items.note: Often implies escaping pursuit, detection or a duty; can suggest deliberate evasive behaviour.

items.pt: fugir; escapar de um local fechado
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: Three prisoners broke out during the night but were caught the next morning.
items.note: Here break out means escape from confinement; noun: a breakout. Different from disease breaking out.

items.pt: fuga em massa; evasão de prisão
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The prison breakout prompted an urgent security review.
items.note: A noun for an escape from prison or detention; compare outbreak for disease or violence.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: A mysterious illness broke out in several villages after the floods.
items.note: A disease or conflict can break out suddenly; the related noun is outbreak.

items.pt: surto; início repentino de doença ou violência
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: Health officials investigated an outbreak of food poisoning.
items.note: Used especially for disease, war or violence; contrasts with a prison breakout.

items.pt: ficar atento a; procurar sinais de
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: Investors are looking out for early signs of economic recovery.
items.note: Pay attention in order to notice something; also warn someone to watch for danger.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The economic outlook improved slightly after the new figures were released.
items.note: Prospects or expectations, especially about the future; not a person keeping watch.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: One member of the group acted as a lookout while the others entered the building.
items.note: A person watching for danger or police; distinct from outlook, a future prospect.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: An independent committee will look into the complaint.
items.note: Examine or investigate a problem; distinct from look out for something.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The institute set up a new laboratory to test electronic sensors.
items.note: Verb phrase meaning establish or arrange; the noun is setup, written as one word.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The new management setup gives each regional office more independence.
items.note: A noun describing how a system or organisation is arranged; not written as set up.

items.pt: colocar de pé; virar para uma posição vertical
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: They upended the sofa so it would fit through the doorway.
items.note: Verb with up- before the root; here it means raise or turn into a vertical position.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: We took the wrong exit and ended up in a neighbouring town.
items.note: The particle follows the verb; describes an eventual or unintended outcome.

items.pt: confirmar; manter uma decisão; defender um princípio
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The appeal court upheld the original ruling.
items.note: A formal verb for supporting or confirming a decision, law or principle.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: A signal failure held up the train for almost an hour.
items.note: Here the particle follows the verb and means delay; distinct from uphold a decision.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The younger competitor managed to outdo the reigning champion.
items.note: Do better than another person or previous result; out- comes before the root.

items.pt: redecorar; reformar a decoração de um espaço
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: They plan to do out the kitchen before putting the flat on the market.
items.note: Informal British usage for decorating or refurbishing a room; different from outdo.

items.pt: correr mais rápido que; ultrapassar em velocidade
items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The athlete managed to outrun his rivals in the final hundred metres.
items.note: Means run faster than someone or something; not the same as run out.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: Our printing supplies ran out just before the deadline.
items.note: If a supply runs out, nothing remains; with a possessor, use run out of something.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: The sudden cancellation upset everyone who had travelled for the meeting.
items.note: Here upset is a verb meaning make someone worried or unhappy; distinct from set up.

items.section: C · Phrasal verbs, nouns and particle order
items.example: She missed the morning meeting because of a stomach upset.
items.note: Exercise-only noun sense of upset: a minor digestive disturbance, not an emotional reaction.
